mainEntity.name: How long should a dental crown last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a dental crown depends on the material used, the location of the tooth, the patient's oral hygiene habits, and whether they grind their teeth. In general, well-maintained crowns can last ten to fifteen years or longer. All-ceramic and zirconia crowns have improved considerably in durability. Regular dental check-ups are important to monitor the condition of the crown and detect any early signs of wear or margin breakdown. Your dentist can advise on the expected longevity of a specific restoration based on your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Can decay develop under a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, secondary decay beneath a dental crown is possible. Bacteria can enter through microscopic gaps at the margin where the crown meets the natural tooth, particularly if the cement has deteriorated or oral hygiene is not optimal. This is one of the reasons why regular dental check-ups and X-rays are important even when a crown appears to be intact. If decay is detected beneath a crown, the old crown will need to be removed, the decay treated, and a new crown placed — or, if the tooth is too compromised, alternative options may be discussed.

Crown replacement is typically carried out under local anaesthetic, so the procedure itself should not be painful. Some patients experience mild sensitivity or tenderness around the treated tooth in the days following the appointment, particularly if the underlying tooth required additional work. If significant discomfort persists beyond a few days, it is worth contacting your dentist. Your dental team will always aim to ensure you are comfortable throughout the procedure and will discuss pain management options with you beforehand.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible to repair a crown rather than replace it?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, minor chips or surface damage to a crown can be repaired using composite resin material, particularly if the structural integrity of the crown is otherwise sound. However, this is not suitable for all situations. If the crown is significantly damaged, the margin has broken down, there is decay beneath, or the crown is very old, full replacement is usually the more appropriate clinical option. Your dentist will assess the crown and advise on the most suitable course of action following examination. You can also read can a crown be polished and when is that appropriate for related context.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I delay replacing a crown that needs replacing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Delaying replacement of a crown that has been clinically assessed as needing attention may allow any underlying problems — such as decay or infection — to progress. In some cases, this could make subsequent treatment more complex. If the underlying tooth deteriorates significantly, it may no longer be able to support a new crown, and alternative options such as extraction and implant placement or bridgework may need to be considered. Seeking timely dental advice is always the most prudent approach when concerns arise.

mainEntity.name: Will my new crown look natural?

acceptedAnswer.text: Modern dental crowns — particularly those made from all-ceramic materials or zirconia — are designed to closely replicate the appearance of natural tooth enamel in both colour and translucency. Your dentist or dental technician will work to match the shade and shape of the new crown to your surrounding teeth. Results will vary depending on the material chosen, the skill of the dental team and laboratory, and individual tooth anatomy. Your dentist will discuss realistic aesthetic expectations with you during the planning stages of treatment.
